newsitem.title: BRAZIL: MALAN SHAMED BY BRAZIL'S SOCIAL INJUSTICE.
newsitem.headline: MALAN SHAMED BY BRAZIL'S SOCIAL INJUSTICE.

text.p: Hyperinflation may have been defeated and Brazil may be on the path to economic stability, but Finance Minister Pedro Malan can only feel shame when he thinks of the country's iniquitous distribution of wealth.

In a speech to deputies to mark the third anniversary of the "Plano Real" economic stabilization plan, Malan noted Brazil was the world's fifth most populous country and among its 10 largest economies.
"Yet in terms of per capita income and wealth distribution, we are way down the list, which makes me hang my head in shame before visitors," Malan said.
"The degree of inequality in Brazil is unacceptable," he added. "You can't solve this with campaign speeches. And you can't solve this in one or two years."
The government says the Plano Real has turned 13 million poor into consumers for the first time. But human rights groups say 30 million still live in squalid poverty.

A United Nations report last year placed Brazil bottom of the table for distribution of wealth. For example, while police recruits scrape by on about $250 a month, a handful of police colonels make $30,000 a month.

Malan was addressing the Chamber of Deputies' Economy, Industry and Commerce Committee, which is hosting a series of presentations by top government economic officials over the next two weeks to mark the Plano Real's third birthday back in July.

In a one hour speech that skirted controversial issues like the strong exchange rate, the finance minister said inflation, which touched a high of some 3,000 percent just a few years ago, should plunge to six percent this year.
Malan said 1997 would be the fifth successive year of gross domestic product growth, projected at four percent.
He said two "fundamental challenges" remained -- stabilizing the external accounts, which groups trade in merchandise and services, and balancing the public sector's books.

Malan reiterated that Brazil's widening current account gap -- now at 4.2 percent of GDP -- was natural for a developing country needing to import capital and that high inflows of long-term foreign capital would finance the deficit.
"Our current account gap is not expanding explosively. We would not allow that to happen and we have the tools to keep it under control," he said.

On the fiscal front, Malan said the consolidated public sector nominal deficit, also called the Public Sector Borrowing Requirement, had shrunk to 5.5 percent of GDP in the 12 months to May compared to 7.8 percent in the same period a year ago.
With privatizations, cost rationalizations and the slow but ongoing passage of pension and civil service reforms through Congress, "We are taking steps in the right direction", he said.
But the finance minister returned repeatedly to social injustice, noting the most important role for government was to "invest in people" through basic education and health.
Malan said social injustice was a legacy of colonialism, empire and slavery, followed by decades of military rule that centralized political and economic power.
